summary: Describes an architecture for admission and termination of flows based on pre-congestion information, to protect the quality of service of established inelastic flows such as voice inside a single Diffserv domain.

plainLanguage.summary: A road can warn drivers before it becomes jammed. This note describes how a network can use early warnings to stop new calls or end some, so existing calls stay clear.

subtitle: An early-warning scheme that lets a Diffserv network admit new real-time flows only when there is room, and shed a few when things go wrong.

tldr.problem: Operators want to protect the quality of service of inelastic flows such as voice inside a single Diffserv domain, without keeping per-flow state in every router and without relying on static, conservative traffic predictions.
tldr.mechanism: Every link meters the bulk of PCN-traffic against two configured rates below the link rate and marks packets when they are exceeded. Boundary nodes read the marks at the egress and use them to block new flows (admission control) or terminate some existing flows (flow termination).
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture document. It describes the functions, assumptions and open issues, and leaves the metering algorithms, encodings and boundary-node behaviours to companion documents.

today: RFC 5559 is an Informational RFC from June 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the architecture only; the metering algorithms, encodings and boundary-node behaviours are specified in companion documents.

sections.title: The Idea of Pre-Congestion Notification
sections.content:
The objective of Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) is to protect the QoS of inelastic flows within a Diffserv domain in a simple, scalable and robust fashion. Two mechanisms are used: admission control, which decides whether to admit or block a new flow request, and, in abnormal circumstances, flow termination, which decides whether to terminate some existing flows.

Each link meters the overall rate of PCN-traffic and marks PCN packets when certain configured rates are exceeded. These rates are below the link rate, so boundary nodes are warned about overload before any congestion occurs, hence the name. The name is by analogy with ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification). The two configured rates are the PCN-threshold-rate and the PCN-excess-rate.

PCN-ingress-nodes police arriving packets against the admitted flows, so they keep per-flow state. PCN-interior-nodes meter all PCN-traffic together and need no per-flow state. Decisions are made per pair of boundary nodes, so egress nodes must be able to tell which ingress node sent each PCN packet. Compared with hop-by-hop IntServ, per-flow state is only needed at ingress nodes. Compared with plain Diffserv, the operator can be less accurate and conservative in predicting the traffic matrix.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a road that flashes a yellow light when it is getting busy, before any traffic jam. The people at the entrance see the light and stop letting new cars in, and if things get really bad they send a few cars home.

sections.title: Interior Nodes, Boundary Nodes and the Two Rates
sections.content:
Functionality is split. PCN-interior-nodes monitor their own pre-congestion and mark packets; they are not flow-aware. PCN-boundary-nodes at the edge of the PCN-domain control admission and termination, using the marked data packets themselves rather than signalling messages. The aim is to keep the bulk of the network simple, scalable and robust, and confine policy, application-level and security interactions to the edge.

Each link runs two metering behaviours. Threshold-metering marks all PCN packets whenever the PCN-traffic rate is above the PCN-threshold-rate. Excess-traffic-metering marks a proportion of packets such that the marked amount equals the traffic rate above the PCN-excess-rate. The threshold-rate is lower than the excess-rate. Admission control limits PCN-traffic to roughly the PCN-admissible-rate, and flow termination limits it to roughly the PCN-supportable-rate. With three encoding states these are configured equal to the threshold-rate and excess-rate respectively.

Marking is done by changing the DSCP and ECN fields. In the baseline encoding the ECN field is set to 11 and the DSCP is not altered, which gives two states: not PCN-marked and PCN-marked. Extended encodings can give three states: not PCN-marked, threshold-marked and excess-traffic-marked. An operator may deploy admission control, flow termination or both. With only two encoding states, the options are admission control only, flow termination only, or both from a single marking by setting the excess-rate equal to the admissible rate, at the cost of less accurate admission control.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the network, helpers only count how busy each road is and put a sticker on packets when it is too busy. Only the helpers at the doors, who know which call is which, decide who gets in or out.

sections.title: Admission, Termination and Node Functions
sections.content:
For admission, the PCN-egress-node measures, for a particular ingress-egress-aggregate, the fraction of PCN-traffic that is threshold-marked, possibly as a moving average. If the fraction is below a threshold the flow is admitted, otherwise it is blocked. Another approach is to block new flows if one or several threshold-marked packets arrive. The decision may be made at the egress node, recommended by the egress node and made by the ingress node, made at the ingress node, or made at a centralised node.

For termination, one approach compares the rate of PCN-traffic that is not excess-traffic-marked, measured at the egress, with the rate sent towards that egress, measured at the ingress; the difference is what should be terminated. Another measures the excess-traffic-marked rate and terminates that amount. A third picks at random from the flows that have an excess-traffic-marked packet, because terminating all of them would remove far too much traffic.

Interior nodes classify the behaviour aggregate, meter, mark and drop. Ingress nodes classify, police (dropping PCN-packets that do not belong to an admitted flow, and checking flows stay within their flowspec), PCN-colour and sometimes meter. Egress nodes classify by ingress node, meter and PCN-colour, resetting the ECN field to 00 in the baseline encoding. In-band marks carry the pre-congestion information; signalling, for example an extension of RSVP or NSIS, carries the feedback between boundary nodes.

The RFC also gives a worked example using RSVP end to end, where the PCN-domain is a single RSVP hop and PCN-traffic uses expedited forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: For letting people in, the door helper checks how many stickers arrived on recent packets. For sending some home, they work out how much extra traffic there is and end just enough calls to fix it.

sections.title: Tunnels, Faults and Operations
sections.content:
Tunnels inside a PCN-domain follow the uniform model of RFC 2983: any PCN-marking is copied into the outer header on encapsulation, and on decapsulation the outer marking is copied inward if it is more severe. The order of severity is not PCN-marked, threshold-marked, excess-traffic-marked. For a tunnel with only one end in the domain, the inner PCN-marking is cleared at the tunnel end that lies inside the PCN-domain (the egress if the tunnel starts outside, the ingress if it ends outside). Tunnelling constraints were a major factor in choosing the baseline encoding: with current tunnel endpoints only the 11 codepoint of the ECN field survives decapsulation.

If an interior node or link fails, routing re-routes around it. If the new route cannot carry everything, PCN admission blocks new flows and flow termination may take effect. For operations, the RFC covers configuration (a MIB with SNMP is one possibility), accounting (out of scope, since it is done at trust boundaries), and provisioning: the volume of PCN-marking per queue is described as an early-warning metric for upgrades, needing just three counters per PCN queue for threshold markings, excess-traffic markings and drops. Operators should regularly test that blocking and termination still work, since they are rarely used.
sections.plainLanguage: If a road closes, traffic is rerouted and the warning stickers tell the door helpers to hold new calls. The helpers also keep three tally counters per road so the owners know where to build more lanes.

sections.title: Assumptions, Benefits and Open Issues
sections.content:
The scope rests on four assumptions: a single Diffserv domain where all PCN-nodes are PCN-enabled and trusted; inelastic real-time flows constrained to a known peak rate; enough flows on any bottleneck link for statistical mechanisms to work; and emergency use (such as 911, GETS, WPS and MLPP) out of scope. PCN is unsuitable if sources adapt their rate to pre-congestion, if a bottleneck link has room for only a few flows, or if a flash crowd can arrive within the reaction time of the mechanism.

Listed benefits include a stateless core, admission control that survives re-routes without extra signalling, in-band marking with no extra signalling protocol, and provisioning that is decoupled from adding customers. Flow termination also lets an operator avoid running links at low utilisation to protect against failures.

Open issues the RFC names include ECMP routing (over-admission, under-admission and ineffective termination), tunnelling, bi-directional sessions that should be admitted as a pair, global coordination across ingress-egress aggregates, variable aggregate traffic, flash crowds, and sources that stay silent at the start of a flow. Potential solutions are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This works best when lots of calls share a road, they all need steady traffic, and everyone at the doors can be trusted. It struggles when roads split into many paths or when many callers arrive at the same instant.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security comes mainly from the trust assumption: all PCN-nodes must truthfully meter and mark. The boundary nodes together must encircle the PCN-domain, otherwise packets could enter without admission control and destroy the QoS of existing flows. Ingress nodes must police and drop (or downgrade) PCN packets outside an admitted flow.

Interior nodes are not flow-aware, which prevents some attacks that target specific flows in the data plane. But a rogue interior node could mark every packet so that no flow is admitted, mark none even when pre-congested, or do either selectively. Boundary nodes should withstand DoS and state exhaustion attacks based on fast changes in per-flow signalling, and signalling between boundary nodes must be protected, for example with authentication and protection against replay and man-in-the-middle attacks. Operational advice is given in Section 5.5 of the RFC, which suggests alarms on persistent marking and on anomalies such as marks focused on particular flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who puts stickers on packets must be honest, and the door helpers must keep out cars with no ticket. A cheater who marks wrongly could shut everyone out or let too many in.
